pebbles.title: FloodNet ultrasonic depth sensors (NYC)

narration.short: FloodNet sensors and historical flood events near this address.

provenance.source_name: FloodNet (New York University and The City University of New York)
provenance.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0
provenance.citation: FloodNet street flood sensors. Flood events and sensor status read from the FloodNet Data API (api.floodnet.nyc, an early-access beta) at the retrieval time shown. A flood event is a series of depth measurements greater than 10 mm at the sensor (FloodNet's definition); a depth is measured at one point and does not show the depth on every part of the street. Riprap counts the events the API marks as verified by a person. FloodNet's published cautions about a depth: "most FloodNet sensors are mounted over sidewalks and are thus unable to measure floods in the roadbed until the water rises above the height of the curb"; the depth at the street's lowest point differs from the reading by the sensor's height above that point; "a single anomalous data point, measured during a flood event" may exaggerate a maximum depth; and a sensor may miss a flood "if it was offline and awaiting repair or had not been deployed yet or retired" (FloodNet's NYC Open Data description, dataset aq7i-eu5q). Ten rows of FloodNet's deployments table are NOAA and USGS tide gauges (deploy_type "tidal"); Riprap does not count them as FloodNet sensors. Cite: Mydlarz et al. (2024), Water Resources Research 60, e2023WR036806, https://doi.org/10.1029/2023WR036806; Silverman et al. (2022), Water Research, 118648, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.watres.2022.118648. Licence: FloodNet data and content derived from it are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-sa/4.0/), not Riprap's Apache-2.0. Riprap is independent of FloodNet and not endorsed by it.

dep_extreme_2080.citation: NYC Stormwater Flood Maps (NYC Open Data 9i7c-xyvv, Department of Environmental Protection), map "Extreme Flood (3.66 inches/hr) with 2080 Sea Level Rise". The Stormwater Resiliency Plan (2021) describes its extreme scenario as "approximately 3.5 inches of rain falling in one hour (also referred to as the 100-year storm, with approximately 1 percent chance of occurrence in any given year) combined with 4.8 feet of SLR". Map disclaimer, from DEP's own map items (arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=5b82c08be55d4f30bf28d265ab8e4a49): the map "is intended to be an informational tool and does not provide the exact depth of flooding at any location", shows "the relative risk of flooding in public areas from stormwater runoff due to rain only", and "shall not be used for the design, modification, or construction of improvements to real property or for flood plain determination". The caveat on an outside reading quotes NYC Emergency Management, Hazard Mitigation Plan, flooding profile (https://nychazardmitigation.com/documentation/hazard-profiles/flooding/).
dep_extreme_2080.narrative: The city's stormwater flood map "Extreme Flood (3.66 inches/hr) with 2080 Sea Level Rise" shows no flooding category, at the edge of flooding mapped on it (within about 3 m) at the point mapped for this address. The city's stormwater flood maps are modelled scenarios (each a design storm paired with a sea level), not forecasts: their rainfall flooding categories cover public areas and rain only, the city says the map "does not provide the exact depth of flooding at any location", and it is not a flood plain determination. Outside a mapped extent does not mean safe: NYC Emergency Management reports that during Hurricane Ida in 2021 "The most heavily impacted areas, representing over half of all damaged buildings, were also outside of any flood risk scenario, including FEMA floodplain maps and the NYC Stormwater Resiliency Plan's Extreme and Moderate stormwater scenarios" (NYC Hazard Mitigation Plan, flooding profile, nychazardmitigation.com).

city_landcover.narrative: New York City's 2017 land cover map (6 inch, from LiDAR and aerial imagery) shows that 83.5% of the ground within 500 m of this address is paved or built over and 16.5% is green (11.5% tree canopy).

landcover.narrative: Experimental: a satellite land-cover model estimates that 83.7% of the ground within 500 m of this address is paved or built over and 16.0% is green (9.5% tree canopy), on Sentinel-2 scenes from 2026; no change between years is read from it. Limits: it estimates the share of each 10 m satellite pixel that is canopy, grass, paving, roof, water or bare ground, learned from the city's 2017 six-inch map, so detail finer than about 30 m is blurred and a tree over a street counts as canopy; against The Nature Conservancy's 2021 six-inch map of the city, on squares it never trained on, it read a typical district's paved share 1.7 points above the map's (at most 7.8 points off in the 46 districts with enough test ground) and its mean error per land-cover group was 4.8 points at best, more than the 3.0 points of the city's 2017 map read as if it were 2021, so the 2017 map is the more accurate source for its year; citywide its maps show 4.2 to 5.0 points less tree canopy than the city's 2017 map in 3 of its 4 yearly maps (2018, 2021, 2026) and 3.2 points more in 1 of its 4 yearly maps (2024), which is the model and its images and not the trees, so its canopy share can be several points off; two images of one summer differ by under 2.0 points in a district's paved share 19 times in 20, but between 2018 and 2024 the shares of 49 of 59 districts differ by more, so its maps of different years are not compared. Rely on the city's 2017 land cover map and The Nature Conservancy's 2021 map (both 6 inch) and the city's building footprints for a survey.

By UTC calendar year: 2 in 2025 and 4 in 2026. FloodNet's API lists 8 more events labelled flood here that are still to be verified by a person; Riprap counts verified events only. The highest depth in FloodNet's record for these sensors in that period is 1172 mm (46.1 in) on 2026-05-20, in an event the API marks as verified by a person, at a sensor listed as "noisy" in FloodNet's API when this was read (2026-10-05); that is the sensor's status now, which the API does not give for the day of the event. 1 of the 2 sensors is listed with a status other than "good" in FloodNet's API when this was read ("noisy") and recorded 3 of the 6 events.

nyc311.narrative: 88 NYC 311 flood and sewer complaints filed within 200 m of this location in the last 5 years (since 2021-10-06): 48 sewer backup, 27 catch basin, 10 street flooding, 3 manhole overflow. A count of complaints is a count of reports filed, not of floods: a low count can mean under-reporting and not the absence of flooding, because the propensity to file a 311 request varies with income, language and demographics (studies of other 311 complaint types: Kontokosta, Hong and Korsberg, arXiv:1710.02452; Boxer, Hong, Kontokosta and Neill, Annals of Applied Statistics 19(2), 2025, doi:10.1214/24-AOAS2003).
